title: Three Planets Are Putting on a Show in the Evening Sky—Here's How to Catch It!
summary: Have you noticed two super bright 'stars' in the west after sunset? Those aren't stars—they're planets! Venus and Jupiter are the brightest, and they're getting closer each night. On June 9, they'll be so close you could cover them with just a few fingers held at arm's length. Venus is the brighter one, shining like a silvery-white diamond. Jupiter is also bright but dimmer. Look below them, and you might spot a third planet: Mercury. It's trickier to see because it's small and close to the sun, but right now is a great time to try. About 45 minutes after sunset, look low toward the west-northwest. Find Venus first, then look about one and a half fist-widths below and to the right. Mercury will be there, glowing with a faint yellowish-orange tinge. You don't need a telescope—just your eyes and a clear view of the horizon. The show lasts through late June, so grab your family and go planet-spotting!
why_it_matters: You don't need any special tools—just step outside to see a cosmic dance that humans have marveled at for thousands of years, right from your own neighborhood.

fist-widths: a way to measure distance in the sky by holding out your fist; one fist-width covers about 10 degrees.
silvery: shiny and pale grey-white, like the metal silver.

background_read: Planets shine because they reflect sunlight, not because they make their own light like stars do.
Venus is often called the 'evening star' and is so bright because its thick clouds reflect a lot of sunlight.
Ancient Greeks named Mercury after their speedy messenger god because the planet moves quickly across the sky.
Article_Structure: WHO: Anyone with a clear western view, especially families.
WHAT: A close grouping of Venus, Jupiter, and Mercury visible after sunset, peaking on June 9.
WHERE: Low in the west-northwest direction about 45 minutes after sunset.
WHY: To enjoy a rare planetary gathering that doesn't require equipment and lasts for weeks.

perspectives.description: Excited about the rare chance to spot three planets at once and share the sight with friends and family.
Worry that bright streetlights and buildings will block the view of the low horizon where the planets appear.
Happy that the viewing time is after sunset, so there's no risk of accidentally looking directly at the sun.
